name: Carlos Diaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for your time, Carlos. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say is confidential, so you can tell me your public view and your private one. Could you start with a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on an underground and substation crew for Metro Grid, the power company in a city that's growing like crazy. Half our work right now is new feeders, the big underground cables, out to data centre campuses on the edge of town. I'm at the depot at seven, we load the cable trailer, and then it's pulling cable through vaults, helping terminate it at the switchgear, and a lot of standing around while the journeymen do the dangerous part. I'm an apprentice, and I'm still learning which end of a splice kit is which.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How does someone end up an apprentice at 58?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I was a land surveyor for thirty years, the last ten mostly doing drone mapping and maps on a computer. I got very good at it and very bored. My company got bought, I took a nice payout, and I thought, I've mapped a thousand power line routes, I want to build one. My wife Lucia is a pharmacist and she said go ahead, as long as I don't fall off anything. I use AI every day, I take photos of equipment and ask it what I'm looking at, then I check with Sunil, the jointer who's teaching me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fine, it's a useful tool, and the people who called it the end of the world can calm down. At the depot I'd probably show the guys how I use it for studying and they'd roll their eyes. Online I'd post something about how the power demand from the data centres was real either way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means I keep going. I finish my apprenticeship, I work until 65 or so, and I keep using AI as a smart notebook. Honestly, a world where AI stays a handy tool suits me fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carlos keeps going as he is, with daily AI study and the apprenticeship. He'd keep his utility shares, since the grid gets built either way, and keep showing younger crew how he uses the tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Maybe a touch let down, because I like new toys.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the data centres. What does it look like from the ground?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It looks like copper and concrete. We've put in four new feeders this year to one campus alone, each one thick as my arm. Whatever happens with AI, somebody already paid for those cables, and they're not coming back out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do the guys at the depot react to you using AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sunil thinks it's funny until it's useful. Last month it read a faded nameplate on an old transformer from my photo when none of us could. Now he sends me pictures and asks me to ask it.

S0.say: I'd say it's a useful tool and the people predicting the end of the world can calm down. Online I'd point out that the data centres' power demand was real either way.
S0.think: Privately he keeps going: finish the apprenticeship, work until about 65 and use AI as a smart notebook. A world where AI stays a handy tool suits him.
S0.do: Keeps going with daily AI study and his apprenticeship. Keeps his utility shares, since the grid gets built either way, and shows younger crew how he uses the tools.
S0.feel: Calm, a little let down because he enjoys new tools.
S0.quote: It looks like copper and concrete.
S0.fieldNote: Carlos brings a surveyor's eye to the job and a habit of using AI daily as a study aid. He's practical and unexcitable, seeing the grid build-out as real whatever happens with AI. Small stories, like the faded nameplate, show how he wins over sceptical colleagues.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the normal pace of new technology and people should get on with learning it. At the depot I'd say it's like when surveyors went from tape measures to GPS. Online I'd share practical stuff, how-tos, not opinions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think it's good for me. I'm a weak apprentice but a strong tech user. If Metro Grid brings in drones for vault inspections or AI for planning the cable pulls, I'm one of the people who already speaks that language.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carlos would offer to help Metro Grid trial any drone or sensor system, given his ten years of drone mapping. He'd put another 20,000 into utility and grid equipment shares, betting on the build-out. He might also do some weekend drone survey work for old surveying contacts, for the fun as much as the money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and a bit excited. This is the version where I get to be useful in two ways.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at the depot would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The guys in their forties who aren't comfortable with screens and aren't close to retirement. They've got twenty years left and they'll need to learn. I'd try to help, but you can't make someone want to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a risk you're too relaxed about this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. I've got a payout in the bank, Lucia works, the kids are grown. It's easy for me to be relaxed. I try to remember that when I'm talking to Sunil, who's still paying off a house.

S1.say: I'd say this is the normal pace of new technology, like surveyors going from tape measures to GPS. Online I'd share practical how-tos rather than opinions.
S1.think: Privately he thinks it's good for him: a weak apprentice but a strong tech user. If drones or AI planning arrive, he already speaks that language.
S1.do: Offers to help Metro Grid trial drone or sensor systems, drawing on his drone mapping years. Puts another 20,000 into utility and grid equipment shares and takes some weekend drone survey work for old contacts.
S1.feel: Calm and somewhat excited, seeing himself useful in two ways.
S1.quote: I try to remember that when I'm talking to Sunil, who's still paying off a house.
S1.fieldNote: Carlos sees opportunity and is honest that his security makes calm easy. His worry is for mid-career colleagues with decades left and little comfort with screens. He combines investing in the build-out with offering his drone skills to the company.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is too fast for the grid, never mind people. At the depot I'd say the power has to come from somewhere, so for a while there'll be more work, not less. Online I'd probably say governments need to step in on the transition, because two years is nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm not worried about my money. But I'd be 60 and an unfinished apprentice, and the robots would be terminating cable better than me within a year or two. My useful bit would be the tech side, and that's exactly what AGI does best, so I'm not as special as I thought.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carlos would sell about a third of his general shares and put the money into grid and power companies, guessing that AGI needs electricity. He'd ask Metro Grid to put him on whatever team brings robots into the vaults, even if it meant leaving the apprenticeship. If nothing fitted after a year, he'd retire and live on the payout and Lucia's salary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not scared, but the ground's moving faster than I can plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With only two years' warning, what does the short time change for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means my clever plan of being the tech guy on the crew has a shelf life of about a year. With two years, I'd be making moves on guesses, not on information. That's the part I don't like, I'm a surveyor, I like to measure first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Lucia about her job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pharmacy's interesting, because a lot of it is checking and counting, which a machine would do well. I'd tell her we're fine either way, and she could stop when she likes. She'd probably tell me to worry about myself.

S2.say: I'd say this is too fast for the grid, never mind people, though power has to come from somewhere so there'd be more work for a while. Online I'd say governments need to step in, because two years is nothing.
S2.think: Privately money isn't the worry, but at 60 and unfinished, robots would soon terminate cable better than him. His edge was the tech side, which AGI does best, so he's less special than he thought.
S2.do: Moves about a third of his general shares into grid and power companies, betting that AGI needs electricity. Asks Metro Grid to put him on the team bringing robots into the vaults, and retires on his payout and Lucia's salary if nothing fits after a year.
S2.feel: Uneasy, with the ground moving faster than he can plan.
S2.quote: I'm a surveyor, I like to measure first.
S2.fieldNote: The surprise is Carlos realising that his advantage, tech comfort, is exactly what AGI erodes. Two years forces him to act on guesses, which grates against his surveyor's instinct to measure first. Strong savings keep him from real alarm, and he's quick to invest on a thesis.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to do something smart. At the depot I'd say let's learn what the robots need from us now. Online I'd share what I find out about robot training programmes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years is a good length for me. I'd finish my apprenticeship, then move into robot supervision or grid planning, where line knowledge and tech both matter. I'd be 63 and still interesting to an employer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carlos would finish his apprenticeship in about two years while taking an online robotics course in the evenings. He'd move part of his savings into grid companies gradually rather than all at once. He'd tell Metro Grid early he wants to help lead the robot rollout in the vaults.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Five years lets me measure before I move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still be doing physical line work at the end?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably less. I'd be the one with the tablet, watching the robot do the splice and checking it. I'll miss getting dirty, honestly, I only just started.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your son Andrés?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He's a chef, and I'd tell him a robot might cook the chips but people will pay for his cooking and his company. Then I'd tell him to save more than he does. He'd laugh at me.

S3.say: I'd say five years is enough to do something smart. At the depot I'd say let's learn now what the robots will need from us.
S3.think: Privately five years suits him: finish the apprenticeship, then move into robot supervision or grid planning. At 63 he'd still be interesting to an employer.
S3.do: Finishes his apprenticeship in about two years while taking an online robotics course in the evenings. Moves savings into grid companies gradually and asks Metro Grid early to help lead the robot rollout in the vaults.
S3.feel: Calm, since five years lets him measure before moving.
S3.quote: I'll miss getting dirty, honestly, I only just started.
S3.fieldNote: Five years gives Carlos the time to measure first, which settles him. He'd trade the hands-on work he only just started for a supervisory tablet role, with a little regret. His advice to his son mixes reassurance with a nudge to save.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is good news, enough time to do it right. At the depot I'd say learn the new stuff steadily and don't panic. Online I'd share how-tos and keep out of the arguments.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd do a few years as a journeyman, then retire around 65 in 2033. AGI would arrive after I'm gone. It hardly touches me, apart from wanting to watch it happen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carlos keeps going with his apprenticeship and works as a journeyman until about 65. He'd do weekend drone survey work for fun and a little income, and keep his money spread out without big bets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Curious, mostly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Compared with two years, what does ten change for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years, I'm guessing and moving fast. Ten years, I do the whole thing properly, build some lines, and retire. I'd take ten every time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd regret in this version?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe that I came to the trade so late. With ten years' warning, a young lineworker could plan a whole career around robots. I just get to see the start.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is good news, enough time to do it right. At the depot I'd say learn the new things steadily and don't panic.
S4.think: Privately he'd work a few years as a journeyman and retire around 65 in 2033. AGI arrives after he's gone, so it barely touches him.
S4.do: Keeps going with his apprenticeship and works as a journeyman until about 65. Does weekend drone survey work for fun and a little income, keeping his money spread out without big bets.
S4.quote: Ten years, I do the whole thing properly, build some lines, and retire.
S4.fieldNote: At ten years Carlos is relaxed and makes no big bets, unlike his quick investing in the fast picture. His only regret is coming to the trade so late. The pattern across scenarios is clear: more warning means fewer moves on guesses.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because I'd be making big moves on guesses. What would help is clear information early: what Metro Grid plans to automate and when, and what new roles they'll need. And for the people with twenty years left, proper paid training.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about the power. Everyone talks about AI taking jobs, nobody talks about where the electricity comes from. Every one of these pictures needs more cable in the ground, and right now that's people like me pulling it.

headlineQuote: Every one of these pictures needs more cable in the ground, and right now that's people like me pulling it.
portrait: Carlos Diaz spent thirty years as a land surveyor, the last ten flying mapping drones, before taking a payout and joining Metro Grid's underground crew as an apprentice at 56. He uses AI every day to study and identify equipment, and he's honest that his payout and his wife's salary make it easy to be relaxed. He sees AI driving demand for grid building and invests on that idea. In the fast AGI picture he realises his tech edge won't last and dislikes acting on guesses, while longer timelines let him measure first and retire on schedule.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because he'd be making big moves on guesses rather than information.
whatWouldHelp: Clear early information about what the company plans to automate and what new roles it needs, plus proper paid training for workers with decades left.
